content.text:
Yes, it's a noticeable change, but a controlled one. The color got darker and nothing else moved.

| | `#e94560` | `#bf103f` |
|---|---|---|
| Lightness (OKLCH) | 0.63 | 0.52 |
| Chroma | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| Hue | 15.73° | 15.79° |

- **Lightness dropped by about 0.11.** That's the visible difference. The new color reads as a deeper crimson or raspberry, where the old one was a brighter, livelier coral-red.
- **Hue is essentially unchanged.** It moved 0.06°, which is imperceptible, so it's still the same pink-red family.
- **Chroma is identical.** The color is just as vivid as before. It doesn't look muddy or washed out.

Side by side, most people would see the new one as heavier and less "pop". An 0.11 lightness shift is well above a just-noticeable difference. Brand recognition should hold, though, because hue and saturation are preserved. This is about the smallest change you can make to gain contrast, since the designer only changed lightness.

I didn't run a contrast check, so I haven't confirmed which backgrounds it passes on. If you tell me the background and target ratio, I can check that. I can also see whether a lighter color, closer to the original, would still pass.
